records.table: Laphroaig 10 Year Old is the Islay single malt from the south coast near Port Ellen, ten years in ex-bourbon barrels: peat smoke, seaweed and a medicinal edge over a quiet sweetness. Pour it neat with water beside it, or float a little on a Penicillin.
records.story: Two brothers of the Johnston family set up the distillery on the south coast of Islay, officially in 1815, and their line ran it for more than a century. Ian Hunter (died 1954), by the house's account the last of the Johnston family to run it, took charge in 1908. As the house tells it, he rebuilt the malting floors, took the single malt to America in the years of Prohibition, and brought American ex-bourbon barrels into its warehouses. In 1934 Bessie Williamson (1910 to 1982) came to the island as a typist for the summer. She rose to manage the office, then the distillery, and by 1944 she was running it. When Hunter died in 1954 he left the business to her. From 1962 she sold it in stages to Seager Evans, the firm behind the Long John blend, and she retired in the early 1970s. Through every change the distillery kept its floor maltings and its kiln fired with Islay peat, which are part of why the 10 Year Old tastes as it does. For a bartender it is the bottle that teaches what Islay peat means: smoke, sea and a medicinal edge in one glass.

records.table: Lagavulin 16 Year Old is the Islay single malt from Lagavulin Bay on the south coast, sixteen years in oak and bottled at 43% ABV: deep peat smoke, iodine and seaweed over a slow, dark sweetness. Pour it neat, with a few drops of water if the guest likes.
records.story: Distilling at Lagavulin is older than its paperwork: records suggest illicit stills on the bay by the 1740s, and the house dates its official founding to 1816, when legal distilling began there. In 1878 Peter Mackie (1855 to 1924) came to Lagavulin to join his uncle's firm, and he built his White Horse blend on its malt. His firm was for years the agent for neighbouring Laphroaig; when that agency ended in a quarrel, he built in 1908 a small copy of Laphroaig inside Lagavulin's walls, called Malt Mill, which ran until the early 1960s and whose whisky went mostly into blends. After Mackie's death his company took the name White Horse Distillers and soon joined the Distillers Company. When Malt Mill closed, its stills were moved into Lagavulin's own still house, as the sources tell it. The 16 Year Old was long sold as the Islay malt of the Classic Malts range, and in 2016 the distillery marked two hundred years. For a bartender it is the slow Islay: a long ferment, slow stills and sixteen years in oak round the smoke without taming it.

records.story: Ardbeg dates its founding to 1815, when the MacDougall family took up legal distilling on the south coast of Islay, though spirit was probably made on the site before then. Hiram Walker took control at the end of the 1970s, and in 1981 the distillery closed. It reopened in 1989, but through the 1990s it worked only in spells. In 1997 Glenmorangie bought Ardbeg, and limited distilling began again that June, with full production in 1998. In 2000 the house launched Ardbeg Ten Years Old, and in the same year founded the Ardbeg Committee, a club of followers formed, as the house tells it, so that the doors would never close again. The Ten became the cornerstone of the range. For a bartender it is the Islay malt that shows heavy peat and bright fruit together: the purifier on the spirit still sends the heavier oils back, so the smoke arrives with citrus rather than tar.

records.table: Bowmore 12 Year Old is the Islay single malt from the village of Bowmore on Loch Indaal, partly malted on its own floors and aged in bourbon and sherry casks: lemon, honey and a gentle smoke. It is the soft way into Islay for a guest wary of peat.
records.story: Bowmore gives 1779 as its founding year, though some accounts find no sure sign of licensed distilling there before 1816, and by one account a merchant named Simson, who came to Bowmore in 1766, began it soon after his arrival. In the nineteenth century the Mutter family of Glasgow took it over and built its name in the trade. It passed through several hands in the twentieth century. In 1963 a firm of whisky brokers bought it, and Suntory, which took a share of that business in 1989, completed its purchase in 1994. Through every change the distillery kept its floor maltings, where part of the barley is turned by hand and dried over peat, and its No. 1 Vaults, a warehouse set partly below sea level on the shore of Loch Indaal. For a bartender the 12 Year Old is the middle of Islay: smoke, but with honey and lemon ahead of it, the bottle for a guest taking a first step toward peat.

records.table: Caol Ila 12 Year Old is the Islay single malt from the Sound of Islay near Port Askaig: fresh and sweet, with citrus and a lighter, oily smoke. Much of its malt has long gone into blends such as Johnnie Walker, so many guests have tasted it unknowingly.
records.story: Caol Ila takes its name from the Gaelic for the Sound of Islay, the strait between Islay and Jura that the distillery looks across. It was founded in 1846 in a tight bay beside Port Askaig, on the island's east coast, and changed hands within a few years. In 1863 the blenders Bulloch Lade took it over, and Caol Ila stayed with them until the firm failed in 1920. In 1927 the Distillers Company gained control, and the distillery ran on until 1972, when the old buildings were pulled down, all but one warehouse. A new distillery opened in 1974 with six stills, three times the two it had before, in a still house walled in glass that faces the Sound. For decades nearly all of its malt went into blends, Johnnie Walker among them, and the 12 Year Old is the bottling that lets a guest meet it alone. For a bartender it is the Islay a guest has often tasted without knowing it: lighter and oilier in its smoke than the south coast malts, and the plain way to show how Islay seasons a blend.

cards.answer: Six copper pot stills, three times the two it had, in a still house walled in glass facing the Sound.

quiz.q: A guest looking at Caol Ila's glass still house asks how many stills make the 12 Year Old. How many work there?
quiz.explain: Caol Ila was rebuilt between 1972 and 1974 with six copper pot stills, three times the two it had before the rebuild.

quiz.q: A guest asks what the Gaelic name of Caol Ila means. What does it name?
quiz.explain: Caol Ila means the Sound of Islay, the strait between Islay and Jura; the distillery stands on it, in a bay near Port Askaig.

sources.title: Difford's Guide: Caol Ila Distillery, history

report: The plan's note is settled for the strength: the producer's page gives 43%. The share kept as single malt is left out, as the note allows (Scotchwhisky.com gives about 95 per cent to blends, one source).

Hector Henderson, whom the plan names as founder, is not named in the record: no two sources read gave his death. The year 1846 and the bay beside Port Askaig stand in Wikipedia, Scotchwhisky.com and the producer.

The 1863 purchase by Bulloch Lade stands in Wikipedia and Scotchwhisky.com's Bulloch Lade page; Scotchwhisky.com's Caol Ila page gives 1857, so the record keeps 1863. The 1927 Distillers Company control stands in Wikipedia and Scotchwhisky.com. The rebuild (demolished 1972, reopened 1974, two stills to six, one old warehouse kept) stands in Scotchwhisky.com and Difford's.

The year of the 12 Year Old's first release is left out: Scotchwhisky.com gives 2002 and no second source read confirmed it, so the story says only that the 12 gave the house a standing bottling. The cask type of the 12 was not found on the producer's page and is left out.
The style's own page names Caol Ila among its houses and says nothing that disagrees with this record.

story: the demolition of all but one warehouse in 1972 rests on Scotchwhisky.com and Difford's as the author read them; one search summary called the rebuild an expansion.
